cost-018.explanation: AWS Budgets supports alerts on forecasted cost and Budget actions that automatically apply an IAM policy/SCP or stop EC2/RDS when a threshold is exceeded, with no code. Cost Explorer requires manual review. Cost Anomaly Detection detects anomalies, does not use fixed thresholds, and does not apply policies. A CloudWatch billing alarm + Lambda works but must be written by hand and takes more operational effort.

cost-019.explanation: CUR 2.0 via AWS Data Exports provides the most detailed billing data (hourly, per resource, with tags) into S3, queried with Athena and visualized with QuickSight. Cost Explorer does not provide detailed resource-level data for SQL, and daily manual downloads take effort. Trusted Advisor is a best-practice check. Pricing Calculator only estimates.

cost-020.explanation: A tag appears in Cost Explorer/CUR only after it is activated as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console of the management account (data counts from the activation time). AWS Config checks tag compliance but does not make tags appear in cost reports. Recreating resources is unnecessary. A budget does not help group costs by tag while the tag is not activated.

cost-021.explanation: Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to detect unusual spend and analyze root causes, needs no thresholds, and sends alerts via SNS or email. Budgets requires fixed thresholds. Trusted Advisor checks best practices and does not track cost fluctuations. Compute Optimizer only recommends right-sizing.

cost-022.explanation: Consolidated billing in AWS Organizations combines bills, combines usage to reach lower pricing tiers, and shares RIs/Savings Plans across accounts. Buying RIs separately in each account cannot be shared unless the accounts are in the same organization. Billing Conductor creates pro forma bills for showback/chargeback and does not replace consolidated billing. Control Tower sets up a landing zone; there is no need to recreate the accounts.

cost-023.explanation: Trusted Advisor has cost optimization checks such as unassociated Elastic IPs, idle load balancers, and underutilized EBS; the Enterprise Support plan includes the full set of checks. Pricing Calculator only estimates. Inspector scans for security vulnerabilities. CloudTrail records API calls.

cost-024.explanation: Cost Explorer has coverage reports (how much usage is covered) and utilization reports (how much of the commitment was used), plus Savings Plans purchase recommendations based on past usage. CloudWatch Logs Insights analyzes application logs. Config conformance packs check configuration compliance. Service Catalog manages approved IT products.

cost-025.explanation: AWS Billing Conductor creates pro forma bills with custom billing groups and pricing rules, suited to resellers or showback/chargeback, without affecting the real bill. Cost Anomaly Detection detects unusual spend. Budgets tracks thresholds. Cost Explorer forecasting predicts actual cost and does not create bills with custom prices.

cost-026.explanation: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 is free, and traffic to S3 goes through the endpoint instead of NAT, so NAT processing charges disappear. An interface endpoint has hourly and per-GB charges, so it is not as cheap. A NAT instance adds operational effort and has bandwidth limits. Moving to public subnets reduces security and incurs public IPv4 charges.

cost-027.explanation: CloudFront caches content at the edge, transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free, and CloudFront egress pricing is usually lower than direct egress from S3, while also reducing latency. Transfer Acceleration optimizes uploads and costs extra. Global Accelerator does not cache and has additional charges. Cross-Region Replication incurs replication costs and stores multiple copies.

cost-028.explanation: Instance Scheduler on AWS automatically starts/stops EC2 and RDS on a tag-based schedule, cutting most of the off-hours compute cost with no manual work. RIs are billed 24/7, which wastes money for resources that run only about 50 hours/week. Spot does not apply to RDS and can be interrupted. Manual stopping is easy to forget and takes effort.

cost-029.explanation: gp3 is cheaper per GB than gp2 and has a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of size; a 100 GB gp2 volume has only about 300 IOPS baseline. Elastic Volumes changes the volume type with no downtime. st1 is HDD, unsuitable for random IOPS, and cannot be used as a boot volume. io2 is much more expensive. EFS costs more per GB and requires application changes.

cost-030.explanation: DynamoDB on-demand is billed per request, needs no capacity planning, and fits unpredictable load with long idle periods. Reserved capacity requires a long-term commitment for steady load. Auto Scaling with a high minimum still pays when idle and reacts slowly to sudden spikes. The Standard-IA table class lowers storage price and does not address the capacity problem.

cost-031.explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 scales ACUs automatically with load and charges only for the capacity actually used, which suits load concentrated in a few hours each month; changes are minimal since it is still Aurora PostgreSQL. RIs suit steady 24/7 load; here you would still pay for idle time. Adding replicas increases cost. Moving to DynamoDB requires redesigning the application.

cost-032.explanation: SQS decouples the web and processing tiers, letting workers process at their own pace instead of being provisioned for peak. Scaling on backlog per instance and using Spot for idempotent workers cuts compute cost sharply. Increasing instance size raises cost. Dedicated Hosts are more expensive. An ALB with sticky sessions does not solve provisioning for peak.

cost-033.explanation: Since February 2024 AWS charges for every public IPv4 address, including attached Elastic IPs. Moving instances to private subnets, administering through Session Manager (no public IP or bastion needed), and accessing S3 through a free gateway endpoint eliminates the public IPs. In-use Elastic IPs are still charged. An NLB with a public IP per instance does not reduce the number of public IPs. Global Accelerator has its own charges and is unnecessary.

cost-034.explanation: Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory; raising memory for a CPU-intensive task usually cuts run time sharply and can lower the total cost. Lambda Power Tuning helps find the optimal configuration. Moving to EC2 adds operational effort and is not necessarily cheaper. Increasing the timeout only extends billed time. Provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts but increases cost.

cost-035.explanation: Athena is billed by data scanned. Compressed columnar Parquet reads only the needed columns, and partitioning by date skips irrelevant data; both sharply reduce data scanned. Athena cannot query objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval directly. RDS for several TB of logs costs more and takes more operational effort. Transfer Acceleration is unrelated to queries.

cost-036.explanation: Redshift Serverless scales automatically and charges for compute only while queries run, which suits sporadic load and requires no cluster management. A provisioned cluster with reserved nodes is billed continuously, even when idle. RDS MySQL is not a data warehouse. EMR running continuously costs more and takes much operational effort.

cost-037.explanation: ElastiCache caches repeated read query results, reducing CPU load on RDS and often allowing a smaller, cheaper DB instead of scaling the DB up very large. Scaling the instance class costs much more. Multi-AZ increases availability but does not reduce read load (the standby does not serve reads). Migrating to Aurora takes effort and does not solve the repeated-query problem.

cost-038.explanation: 500 TB over a 100 Mbps link takes more than a year even using the full bandwidth, so it must be moved offline with Snowball Edge. Direct Connect takes several weeks to set up, has fixed fees, and still could not finish in 1 month. DataSync or Transfer Acceleration over the existing link is limited by bandwidth.

cost-039.explanation: FSx for Lustre scratch is cheap and high-performance for temporary processing, links to S3 as a data repository, and can be created/deleted for each run so you pay only while in use. Persistent running all week charges continuously for 50 TB. EFS does not reach Lustre's HPC performance and costs more per GB. EBS io2 is very expensive and is not a shared file system.

cost-040.explanation: FSx for Windows File Server HDD storage is cheaper than SSD for infrequently accessed file shares, and data deduplication reduces stored capacity when there are many duplicate files; SMB and Active Directory integration are preserved. EFS is NFS and does not support SMB for Windows. Self-managing EBS on EC2 adds operational effort and loses managed features. FSx for Lustre is for HPC on Linux, not SMB.

cost-041.explanation: Sparse, bursty traffic that is idle most of the time with short requests is the textbook case for Lambda + API Gateway: you pay only per request and duration, nothing while idle. EC2 On-Demand and an always-on Fargate service both pay during idle time. A 1-year Reserved Instance commits to an instance that is barely used, which is wasteful.

cost-042.explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply automatically to Fargate, Lambda and EC2, so the discount stays as workloads move between compute types. EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply only to EC2 and do not discount Fargate/Lambda. Fargate Spot can be reclaimed with a 2-minute warning, which is not acceptable for an application that must not be interrupted.

cost-043.explanation: A capacity provider strategy lets you keep a base of 2 tasks on FARGATE (never reclaimed) and split the rest by weight, mostly onto the much cheaper FARGATE_SPOT. Running everything on Fargate Spot could lose both required tasks during reclamation. Dedicated Instances cost more and are unnecessary. EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not apply to Fargate.

cost-044.explanation: AWS Batch supports a Spot compute environment with the SPOT_PRICE_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED allocation strategy, multiple instance types for pool diversity, and a retry strategy to rerun interrupted jobs, so it is cheap with little operations work. Reserved Instances do not fit weekly fluctuating batch load. A self-built scheduler adds operational overhead. Lambda is limited to 15 minutes and does not suit long simulations.

cost-045.explanation: Pulling work from SQS and deleting the message only on completion lets the message reappear after the visibility timeout for another worker if the instance is reclaimed; checkpointing to S3 lets the job resume from the latest point instead of restarting. Reserved Instances give up the Spot price benefit. Instance store data is lost when the instance terminates. Raising the max price does not prevent interruptions, which happen mainly because AWS needs the capacity back.

cost-046.explanation: Lambda CPU scales with memory, so a CPU-bound function at 128 MB runs long; more memory can cut duration enough to lower total cost, and Lambda Power Tuning finds the cheapest setting. arm64 (Graviton) has a lower price per GB-second than x86. A shorter timeout makes the function fail midway. Provisioned concurrency adds cost and only reduces cold starts. Moving to EC2 adds operations and is not necessarily cheaper.

cost-047.explanation: Lambda bills duration even while just waiting. A Step Functions Standard workflow is billed per state transition and a Wait state uses no compute, so you pay only for short Lambda invocations that check the status. More memory costs more when the time is mostly waiting. Provisioned concurrency adds a fee. arm64 lowers the unit price but still pays for all the waiting time.

cost-048.explanation: The environments are used about 50 of 168 hours a week, so turning them off after hours (scheduled actions setting the ASG and ECS service to 0) saves the most. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans commit you to paying for hours that are not used. Dedicated Instances cost more.

cost-049.explanation: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 is free and only needs a route table entry, so S3 traffic no longer goes through NAT. An interface endpoint for S3 also avoids NAT but has hourly per-AZ and per-GB fees. A NAT instance adds operational work and still costs money. Transfer Acceleration improves speed and adds a fee; it does not reduce cost.

cost-050.explanation: One NAT gateway per AZ, with each subnet routed to the NAT in its own AZ, removes cross-AZ charges and the single point of failure. Moving everything into one AZ loses high availability. Assigning public IPv4 addresses to every instance adds public IPv4 charges and exposes the instances. A second NAT in the same AZ solves neither problem.

cost-051.explanation: With CloudFront, data from the S3 origin to CloudFront is free, caching reduces origin requests, and Price Class 100 uses only edges in the cheapest areas (North America, Europe), which fits where the users are. Transfer Acceleration and Global Accelerator improve speed but add fees. Cross-Region Replication adds inter-Region and duplicate storage charges and still pays egress.

cost-052.explanation: Direct Connect has an hourly port fee but a lower data transfer out rate than the internet, so for large, steady volumes the total cost is lower, with consistent bandwidth. VPN egress is billed at internet rates; more tunnels do not lower the rate. Transfer Acceleration adds a fee. Transit Gateway adds attachment and processing fees without reducing egress.

cost-053.explanation: ECR images involve the API (ecr.api), the registry (ecr.dkr) and layers stored in S3: interface endpoints for ECR and CloudWatch Logs plus a free S3 gateway endpoint take the traffic off NAT; interface endpoint processing costs less than NAT. Public subnets with public IPs add public IPv4 charges and weaken security. Transfer Acceleration is irrelevant. More NAT gateways do not lower the per-GB processing fee.

cost-054.explanation: VPC peering has no hourly fee and no per-GB processing fee (same-AZ traffic is free), so adding a dedicated peering for the high-volume pair cuts transit gateway charges while other VPCs stay on the TGW. A VPN between VPCs costs money and adds complexity. A second transit gateway still has attachment and processing fees. Going over the internet adds public IPv4 and egress charges and is less secure.

cost-055.explanation: VPC Flow Logs record source/destination IP pairs and bytes; querying them with Athena shows which instances send traffic to other AZs, and Cost Explorer by usage type (DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes) confirms the inter-AZ cost. Trusted Advisor and Compute Optimizer do not analyze network flows. S3 Storage Lens is only for S3.

cost-056.explanation: With an NLB, enabling cross-zone load balancing means traffic to targets in other AZs is billed as inter-AZ transfer. Since targets are already evenly spread per AZ, turning cross-zone off keeps traffic within the AZ while staying balanced and multi-AZ. Global Accelerator adds cost. Putting all targets in one AZ loses HA. More targets do not reduce cross-AZ charges.
